prompt: Threat hunting is best described as…

options.text: Waiting until ransomware encrypts everything, then reacting
Turning off monitoring to reduce noise
Proactively searching for vulnerabilities and threats (patches, firewall changes, new CVEs) before attackers exploit them

explanation: Find and fix weaknesses first — track announced vulns, patch, tune firewall rules, keep systems current.

prompt: Why is identifying an attack early still challenging even with good planning?

options.text: Attacks always send a formal email first
It’s hard to spot an attack until it’s actually occurring — so prevention and monitoring matter

explanation: You want to prevent attacks, but detection is still hard until activity starts — keep systems updated and monitored.

prompt: Automated monitoring tools help incident planning by…

options.text: Identifying and stopping certain attacks even when nobody is actively watching
Removing the need for any training

explanation: Automation covers gaps when staff aren’t staring at dashboards — still part of a layered plan.

prompt: A company wants a light first test of its IR procedures without pulling a full DR weekend. Best choice?

options.text: Skip testing until after a real ransomware event
Run a tabletop exercise around one clear scenario
Immediately fail over the entire production site
Only email the CEO a PDF of the policy

explanation: Tabletops are the lighter, faster way to evaluate processes before investing in full-scale drills.

prompt: After a phishing simulation, several users clicked. The MOST useful next step is…

prompt: NIST Special Publication 800-61 is primarily a guide for…

Computer security incident handling across the full lifecycle

prompt: Which NIST incident-handling phase happens before any attack is underway?

prompt: An incident “go bag” is most useful because it…

Replaces the need for any policies
Is only used for employee onboarding

prompt: Which set belongs in preparation resources for incident response?

Unused sticky notes with admin PINs

So compromised systems can be replaced with trusted software during recovery

A scheduled Microsoft Patch Tuesday calendar entry
A single failed login from the user’s desk

prompt: When an attack is confirmed underway, the priority Messer emphasizes is to…

Only act after a week of observation
Stop the attack as quickly as possible — don’t wait to “see what they do”

prompt: What is a sandbox used for during incident response?

A closed environment to run suspicious code and observe what it changes
A public share for all malware samples

prompt: Recovery after an incident commonly includes all of the following EXCEPT…

options.text: Restoring from known-good backups or install media
Leaving attacker-created accounts active for convenience
Fixing the vulnerability that allowed entry

prompt: When should a post-incident meeting ideally happen?

options.text: Only after waiting a year so emotions cool
As soon as possible after the incident is resolved, while details are fresh

options.text: Did we miss any early indicators — and should monitoring change?

How can we delete all logs permanently?
Can we skip training next year?

prompt: Why must incident-response training happen before a live incident?

options.text: Once an incident is underway, it’s too late for on-the-job training
Training is illegal during business hours

prompt: Which pairing matches the video’s emphasis?

options.text: Preparation = go bag & policies; Detection = alerts/logs; Recovery = reimage & fix vulns; Post-incident = lessons learned ASAP

All phases are the same as passwordless login

prompt: Firewall logs are especially useful because they commonly show…

options.text: Source/destination IPs, ports, and whether traffic was allowed or blocked

prompt: Endpoint logs can include all of the following EXCEPT…

prompt: Why roll endpoint, firewall, and other logs into a SIEM?

options.text: To permanently delete all historical evidence

To replace the need for any firewalls
To correlate events across devices and track a security event end-to-end from one place

prompt: A practical SIEM logging strategy is to…

options.text: Forward every debug message from every toaster on the LAN
Send the log data that matters for security decisions — not necessarily every log line everywhere
Only collect logs after a breach is public

prompt: IPS/IDS log entries commonly describe…

options.text: Known attack types/vulnerabilities (e.g., a SYN flood) with priority and addressing details

prompt: Logs from switches, routers, APs, or VPN concentrators can help identify…

options.text: Routing-table changes, authentication errors, and some network attacks (e.g., SYN floods being blocked)

prompt: Email header metadata can reveal…

options.text: Only the font used in the signature
Servers that handled the message, destination addressing, SPF-related details, and origin path clues

prompt: Photo or Office-document metadata might unexpectedly include…

prompt: Vulnerability scan logs are useful because they can show…

options.text: Missing AV/firewall, open shares, guest accounts enabled, unsupported OS, and known unpatched vulns

prompt: A common problem with automated SIEM reports is that organizations…

options.text: Never have enough data to report on
Can only print them on continuous-feed paper
Are legally banned from reading reports
Generate them but then ignore them in the inbox

prompt: SIEM dashboards are designed mainly to…

options.text: Show current status at a glance (SOC screen), not deep long-term historical compilations

prompt: Packet captures (e.g., Wireshark) add value because they…

options.text: Only list which users changed their desktop wallpaper
Show bit-level traffic detail — headers and payloads across frames — for deep network analysis
Replace the need for any log retention

prompt: The data owner is typically…

options.text: Anyone who ever opened the file
The attacker who stole a copy
Only the intern who files PDFs
A higher-level person broadly accountable for that data set

prompt: The VP of Sales is the data owner for CRM/customer data. Who would most likely own financial data?

prompt: Which statement best describes the data owner’s responsibility?

options.text: Oversee all aspects of that data and remain ultimately responsible for it

explanation: Owners are accountable for the data associated with their role — not just a ceremonial title.

prompt: The data controller primarily…

options.text: Manages how the data will be used and instructs the processor
Physically shreds all hard drives daily

explanation: Controllers decide purpose/use and direct how processors handle the data.

prompt: The data processor primarily…

options.text: Writes the nation’s privacy laws alone
Actually processes or uses the data (often under the controller’s instructions)
Replaces the need for any owner

prompt: Payroll department tells an external payroll company how to run pay. Roles?

options.text: Payroll company = owner; payroll dept = attacker

prompt: A data custodian (or data steward) is mainly responsible for…

options.text: Keeping data secure, accurate, and private — and supporting compliance

prompt: Assigning sensitivity labels and tying them to access control is typically a job for the…

options.text: Only the data processor with no oversight

prompt: Ensuring the organization follows laws/regulations for a data set is most associated with the…

prompt: Why might one organization have both a data owner and a data custodian for the same data?

Owner is ultimately accountable; custodian handles operational security and access day to day

Owners must process every payroll transaction personally

prompt: If a third party processes customer data strictly under your written instructions, that third party is acting as a…

prompt: Security regulations can apply not only to application data but also to…

prompt: From an IT perspective, SOX commonly means…

prompt: HIPAA is primarily concerned with…

prompt: IT security teams need formal processes to…

Report illegal activities according to legal requirements

prompt: A legal hold requires the organization to…

Preserve relevant data so it remains available for future legal proceedings

prompt: Breach disclosure laws typically require organizations to…

options.text: Only notify if printers are offline
Notify about security breaches within legally required time frames for their jurisdiction
Never tell anyone about any breach

prompt: In a medical environment, a common pattern is…

Air-gap every doctor’s phone from the EHR forever with no exceptions

prompt: As organizational scope grows from local/regional to national, security often expands to include…

options.text: Broader confidentiality needs (e.g., national defense, multi-state communication) and stronger protection tech

Global firms never collect citizen data

prompt: Security policies exist primarily to help the organization maintain…

options.text: To revoke access and protect people/property when someone leaves

prompt: Requiring passwords to be stored as salted hashes is an…

prompt: Which statement about org-specific vs published standards is true?

prompt: “Ad hoc” in risk assessment means…

options.text: For this purpose only — a narrow, specific assessment
Every year forever with no scope

explanation: Ad hoc = one specific purpose, then you’re done with that narrow scope.

prompt: The CEO returns from a conference worried about one new attack type and wants a study of just that threat. Best fit?

options.text: Only a tabletop with no risk questions
A mandatory multi-year PCI program with no focus

explanation: Narrow, triggered by a specific concern — classic ad hoc assessment.

prompt: After an ad hoc assessment finishes and reports to leadership, the temporary committee often…

options.text: Disbands — the narrow scope is complete
Must meet daily forever on that same threat only

explanation: Ad hoc work is purpose-built; once done, that committee usually ends.

prompt: Assessments every three, six, or twelve months are…
explanation: Recurring assessments run on a standard schedule and keep ongoing documentation.

prompt: Recurring assessments are often performed…

options.text: Internally by an assessment team (though externals can be used too)

explanation: Many orgs use internal teams on a cadence and maintain continuous records.

prompt: An organization that stores credit card numbers may need an annual risk assessment because of…
explanation: Some assessments aren’t optional — regulations/standards like PCI DSS mandate them.

prompt: A Service Level Agreement (SLA) primarily sets…

options.text: Who owns stock in a partnership
Minimum service terms such as uptime/availability with a provider

explanation: SLAs define measurable service levels — e.g., downtime limits, dispatch, on-site spare gear.

prompt: “No more than four hours of unscheduled downtime, with technician dispatch and on-site spares” belongs in an…
explanation: Those are classic ISP/provider service-level commitments.

prompt: Compared with an MOU, a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA)…

options.text: Is always less detailed than an MOU
Replaces the need for any NDA forever
Is identical to an SLA uptime clause
Adds more detail about the relationship and may include some legal language, but still generally isn’t a full enforceable contract

explanation: MOA is one step above MOU — more detail, still not typically a full contract.

prompt: A Master Service Agreement (MSA) is…

options.text: A legal contract that sets the overall framework/terms for ongoing work between organizations
Only an informal handshake with no billing terms
A unilateral NDA by another name

explanation: MSA covers service terms, billing/payment, etc., as a foundation for future work orders.

prompt: A Statement of Work (SOW) typically includes…

options.text: Only the company’s risk appetite posture
Scope, location, deliverables schedule, and what’s expected for a specific engagement

explanation: SOW details one job so both sides know what “done” means — often paired with an MSA.

prompt: Why pair an SOW with an MSA?

options.text: Because MSAs forbid any future work
So you never need deliverables listed
Reuse the master terms and focus the SOW on this specific set of tasks

explanation: You don’t renegotiate the whole contract for every project — SOW handles the specific work.

prompt: A Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA) is used so parties can…

options.text: Share confidential information (trade secrets, business details) without it spreading to others

explanation: NDAs contractually protect confidentiality before sensitive discussions.

prompt: An NDA that binds only one party to confidentiality is…
explanation: Unilateral = one side must keep secrets; bilateral/mutual = both; multilateral = more than two parties.

prompt: An NDA where both organizations must keep information confidential is…
explanation: Mutual/bilateral NDAs bind both sides — and NDAs are formal signed contracts.

prompt: A Business Partners Agreement (BPA) commonly covers…

options.text: Financial details, ownership stake, decision rights, and what happens if things go wrong

explanation: BPAs document how the partnership works — money, ownership, control, disputes, disasters.

prompt: Two companies want to explore a partnership at a high level before any signed contract. Best starting document?

options.text: MSA with full payment terms only
BPA transferring majority ownership on day one
Bilateral NDA that also sets all SLAs forever

explanation: MOU is the informal, broad starting point; detail and contracts come later (MOA/MSA/BPA as needed).

prompt: Why do organizations perform third-party risk assessments?

options.text: Vendors often hold or touch company data — you need to know how they protect it
Third parties never receive any company data

explanation: Payroll, marketing, travel, materials vendors, etc. share in your data risk — assess them.

prompt: Putting risk-assessment expectations and penalties into the vendor contract mainly ensures…

options.text: Everyone understands requirements and consequences if the agreement is breached
Pentests never need rules of engagement

explanation: Contract language sets clear expectations and penalties for both sides.

prompt: A contract requiring both you and the vendor to run pentests on a schedule is an example of…

options.text: Risk avoidance by never using vendors
Third-party risk controls written into the agreement

explanation: Pentests (often by a specialist firm) can be a contractual risk-assessment requirement.

prompt: Rules of engagement for a pentest primarily define…

options.text: Scope, timing, what’s in/out of bounds, contacts, and how sensitive findings are handled
Which fonts appear in the final report cover

explanation: ROE sets parameters — physical vs internal vs internet tests, hours, IP ranges, emergency contacts, scope.

prompt: A “right to audit” clause in a vendor contract means…

options.text: Audits are only allowed after bankruptcy
You can never review access management
The vendor owns all your data permanently
You may perform regular audits of the vendor’s security controls as agreed

explanation: Right-to-audit puts ongoing audit rights (and often parameters) into the contract.

prompt: Vendor security audits commonly review…

options.text: Only the color of the vendor’s logo
Access management, offboarding, password storage, and VPN access controls
Only the CEO’s favorite sports team

explanation: Audits focus on controls protecting the shared relationship — and should continue over time, not just once.

prompt: Supply chain analysis looks at…

options.text: Security concerns across the path from raw materials to finished product/service

explanation: Every hop in the chain can introduce risk — process, coordination, and technical security between orgs.

prompt: The SolarWinds incident illustrated supply-chain risk because…

options.text: Attackers breached the vendor and shipped malware inside a signed software update to customers

explanation: A trusted, digitally signed update carried malware — classic third-party/supply-chain compromise.

prompt: Independent assessments from outside experts are valuable mainly because they…

options.text: Bring an outside perspective and insights from many other organizations
Replace the need for any contracts

explanation: Internal teams can be too close to their own processes — outsiders see what you miss.

prompt: Due diligence before hiring a third party means…

options.text: Investigating and verifying the company (claims, background checks, interviews) before doing business
Signing first and asking questions never

explanation: Due diligence is pre-deal investigation so you know who you’re trusting.

prompt: Which is a clear conflict of interest with a potential vendor?

options.text: They publish an MTBF for hardware
They work with your biggest competitor, employ an executive’s relative, or offer gifts for signing

explanation: Anything that compromises judgment on either side can block the relationship.

prompt: Ongoing vendor monitoring commonly includes…

options.text: Disabling all logging at the vendor
Only a single audit on day one forever
Financial health checks, IT security reviews, news/social monitoring, and security questionnaires

explanation: Relationships are long-lived — keep monitoring; questionnaires cover DR, data protection, conflicts, etc.

prompt: Vendor questionnaire answers should be…

options.text: Ignored if the logo looks nice
Posted publicly with all customer SSNs
Fed into that vendor’s risk analysis and updated throughout the relationship

explanation: Questionnaire results inform continuous third-party risk analysis.

prompt: Compliance means…

options.text: Meeting a set of required standards (laws/regs and/or agreements with others)

explanation: Compliance is meeting standards — from law, regulation, or contractual agreement.

prompt: Penalties for noncompliance can include…

options.text: Automatic exemption from all future laws
Fines, loss of employment, and in serious cases incarceration

explanation: Noncompliance can be expensive personally and organizationally — up to criminal penalties.

prompt: A Central Compliance Officer (CCO) is typically responsible for…

options.text: Ensuring the organization meets applicable requirements and communicating compliance status

explanation: The CCO owns internal compliance checks and status communication across the org.

prompt: Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) compliance primarily relates to…
explanation: SOX is the Public Company Accounting Reform and Investor Protection Act focus.

prompt: HIPAA compliance is mainly about…
explanation: HIPAA protects health information privacy in the U.S.

prompt: Privacy notices you get from banks/financial institutions are commonly tied to…
explanation: GLBA drives financial privacy disclosures to customers.

prompt: Besides fines, falling out of compliance can also cause…

options.text: Reputational damage, lost licenses, and breached contractual relationships
Automatic air gaps on all systems

explanation: Reputation, licenses to operate/sell, and private contracts can all take hits.

prompt: The Uber breach example mainly illustrates that…

options.text: Hiding a breach instead of disclosing as required can lead to massive fines and personal consequences
NDAs with attackers always solve compliance

explanation: Delayed disclosure and paying attackers to stay quiet backfired — compliance meant announcing properly.

prompt: In compliance monitoring language, due care usually refers to…

options.text: Internal activities showing the organization is acting in good faith

explanation: Due care = internal good-faith compliance work; due diligence = with third parties.

prompt: Due diligence in this video’s framing is associated with…

options.text: Good-faith compliance activities involving third parties

explanation: Messer: internal = due care; third-party-related = due diligence.

prompt: Executive attestation/acknowledgment means…

options.text: No one is responsible for accuracy
The intern deletes the compliance report
An executive signs off that compliance is in good standing (and is accountable for that good faith)
Vendors write your SOX filings alone

explanation: Leadership formally attests — and owns the honesty of that claim.

prompt: Ongoing compliance monitoring is often automated because…

options.text: Large orgs juggle many requirements and need continuous status from people, systems, and third parties
Only one law ever applies to any company

explanation: Automation collects inputs, builds reports, and keeps compliance current.

prompt: Missing a required compliance reporting deadline can result in…
explanation: External compliance often includes scheduled reporting — miss it and you pay.

prompt: Privacy rules can apply at which levels?
explanation: Privacy starts locally and scales up — e.g., local records, national HIPAA, multi-country GDPR.

prompt: GDPR stands for…
explanation: GDPR is the EU’s major privacy regulation affecting people in the EU.

prompt: A key idea of GDPR is that…

options.text: Individuals control what happens with their personal data
Companies may never collect any data

explanation: GDPR puts control back with the person — not only on third parties/companies.

prompt: Under GDPR, a data subject is…

options.text: An identified or identifiable natural person

explanation: Data subjects are people — name, address, genetics, location, etc. can identify them.

prompt: The “right to be forgotten” means…

options.text: A person can request removal of their private data, and the organization must remove it

explanation: Subjects can demand removal of their private information from sites/systems.

prompt: Which of the following is personal data GDPR-style privacy cares about?

options.text: Only the company’s stock ticker symbol
Name, address, photo, email, bank details, social media posts, and similar identifiers

explanation: Lots of everyday identifiers are in scope when they relate to a person.

prompt: The data owner is…

options.text: Only the person who last opened a file
The person with overall responsibility/accountability for that data set

explanation: Owners are senior/business accountable roles — e.g., VP Sales for CRM data.

prompt: In privacy terms, the data controller…

options.text: Replaces the need for any inventory
Manages how the data will be used

explanation: Controllers decide purpose/use; processors actually process the data.

prompt: A payroll department directs a payroll vendor that issues paychecks. Roles?

options.text: Both are only data subjects with no duties
Payroll dept = controller; payroll vendor = processor
Vendor = owner of the whole company; dept = only NDA clerk

explanation: Controller instructs; processor does the work — private data often moves between them (NDAs help).

prompt: A data inventory is…

options.text: A list of firewall ACL comments only
Only a warehouse of physical widgets
A listing of the data an organization collects/stores (owner, update frequency, format, etc.)

explanation: You can’t protect or legally share what you don’t know you hold — inventory first.

prompt: Before sharing data with a third party, privacy practice requires you to…

options.text: Know what’s in your inventory and ensure sharing follows applicable laws/regulations

explanation: Inventory + legal guidelines decide what can leave the organization.

prompt: A cybersecurity audit is useful because it can…

options.text: Examine infrastructure, software, devices, and policies — and find issues before attackers do
Eliminate the need for any policies

explanation: Audits review the environment and controls so you can fix gaps proactively.

prompt: Attestation, in relation to an audit, means…

options.text: An opinion of truth about the audit results

explanation: You audit, then attest to (stand behind) what the audit found.

prompt: Which statement about who performs audits is correct?

options.text: Audits are illegal inside a company
Audits can be internal; some situations also require an external third party

explanation: Internal audits are common; regulations may mandate external oversight.

prompt: Internal audits often help answer questions about…

options.text: Whether compliance tasks are being followed properly

explanation: Internal audits check that the org is actually doing required compliance work.

prompt: An audit committee typically…

options.text: Oversees risk-related audits — including starting and stopping internal audits

explanation: The committee owns that audit governance and often rolls up self-assessments.

prompt: A self-assessment in this context is…

options.text: The organization reviewing its own processes against requirements
A penetration test that always includes physical break-ins

explanation: Self-assessments feed the audit committee’s view of compliance posture.

prompt: When a regulation requires a third-party audit, the organization typically…

options.text: Brings in an external auditor to review records and report status and gaps
Only self-attests with no review ever
Deletes logs before the auditor arrives

explanation: External audits provide independent oversight; frequency/type follow the regulation.

prompt: What usually determines how often an external compliance audit occurs?

options.text: The requirements of the applicable regulation
The color of the badge printer

explanation: Regulation sets audit type and cadence.

prompt: External audit results commonly show…

options.text: That no improvements are ever possible
Where the company stands on compliance today and where it can improve

explanation: Findings = current state + remediation opportunities.

prompt: Why is physical penetration testing important?

options.text: Physical access never matters if there’s a password
Physical access makes it much easier to compromise a system (boot media, modify OS files, etc.)

explanation: With physical access you can alter boot/OS — that’s why data centers lock servers down.

prompt: In a physical pentest, testers typically try to…

options.text: Gain unauthorized entry and explore physical security (doors, windows, elevators, etc.)

explanation: They probe the building’s physical controls every way they can.

prompt: The red team’s role is…

options.text: Offense — attack systems, find vulnerabilities, and try to exploit them

explanation: Red = attackers (authorized).

prompt: The blue team’s role is…

options.text: Defense — detect attacks in real time and block them
Only exploit production with no rules

explanation: Blue = defenders watching and stopping attacks.

prompt: Integrating red and blue teams is valuable because…

options.text: Red finds openings and feeds blue so defenses improve continuously

explanation: Continuous feedback loop hardens the environment.

prompt: A known environment pentest means…

options.text: Testers get full disclosure about the systems they’ll attack

explanation: Known = full info provided up front.

prompt: A partially known environment is often used when…

options.text: The test must never include any scope
You want testers to be sure to attack certain systems while still discovering some things

explanation: Mix of known and unknown — steer testers toward key targets.

prompt: An unknown environment (blind test) means…

options.text: Testers get full network diagrams on day one
Testers get no prior information and must discover everything themselves
Only blue team members may attack

explanation: Unknown/blind = start from scratch.

prompt: Reconnaissance before attacking is used to…

options.text: Replace the need for rules of engagement
Map security tools, servers, apps, networks, and focus on key systems
Skip all planning and attack randomly only

explanation: Recon builds the picture — then you target what matters.

prompt: Passive reconnaissance gathers info…

options.text: Without directly connecting to / querying the customer’s network
Only by ping sweeping the whole subnet
Only by OS fingerprinting on the LAN

explanation: Passive = OSINT-style sources that don’t put your packets on their network.

prompt: Which is an example of passive reconnaissance?

options.text: Reviewing social media, the corporate website, forums, dumpster diving, or talking to partners
Running a port scan against the DMZ

explanation: Those don’t require sending probe traffic into the target network.

prompt: Active reconnaissance is riskier for stealth because…

options.text: You’re sending packets on their network — activity often shows up in logs

explanation: Active queries leave footprints on firewalls and other devices.

prompt: Which is an example of active reconnaissance?

options.text: Only reading the company’s About page
Ping scans, port scans, DNS queries to corporate DNS, or OS/version fingerprinting

explanation: Those actively probe live services/devices.

prompt: A company sends fake phishing emails to employees to see who clicks. This is a…
explanation: Phishing campaigns measure real user susceptibility and drive follow-up training.

prompt: When a user clicks a simulated phishing link, the usual next step is…

options.text: Notify them and assign additional training
Immediately fire them with no training

explanation: Click → awareness correction via online or in-person training.

prompt: Users should look for phishing clues such as…

options.text: Spelling/grammar issues, suspicious domains, odd construction, weird attachments, or credential requests
Only whether the logo is pretty
Only the time the email arrived

explanation: Those inconsistencies are classic phishing tells.

prompt: A well-known organizational process should exist for…

options.text: Reporting suspected phishing emails to the IT security team

explanation: Users must know how and where to report suspicious mail.

prompt: Besides testing users, phishing campaigns can also show whether…

options.text: Email filters are blocking threats before they reach inboxes

explanation: Good filters should catch many phishing attempts before delivery.

prompt: Anomalous behavior recognition looks for…

options.text: Unusual or risky activity on user systems (and related unexpected/unintentional events)

explanation: Catch risky, unexpected, and unintentional behaviors that signal problems.

prompt: Which is an example of risky anomalous behavior?

options.text: Unexpected host-file or core OS file changes, or sensitive files being uploaded out
A scheduled password manager adoption report

explanation: Those changes/uploads can indicate compromise or dangerous activity.

prompt: A login from another country or a sudden spike in data transfers is best categorized as…

options.text: Only a spelling mistake in an email

explanation: Unexpected = not normal for that user/device pattern.

prompt: Misplacing a USB drive or mistyping a domain name is an example of…
explanation: Honest mistakes still matter for awareness and monitoring.

prompt: Security awareness monitoring should typically be…

options.text: Automated — alerts to security and regular metrics reports
Only annual paper memos with no follow-up

explanation: Automation surfaces phishing clicks, MFA adoption, etc., every day.

prompt: If the same user keeps repeating risky behavior after training, awareness teams may…

options.text: Provide extended training and/or adjust that user’s security configurations

explanation: Repeat issues → more training and tighter controls for that person.

prompt: The security awareness team commonly…

options.text: Creates training (role/compliance-specific), communicates via email/posters, and tracks metrics over time

explanation: They own user-facing security education and prove whether it’s working.

prompt: Ideally, users should receive security training…

options.text: Before they connect to the network for the first time
Only after their first major breach
Only when they leave the company

explanation: Train first, then grant access — baseline security understanding up front.

prompt: Why specialize training by department?

options.text: Different roles have different security requirements (e.g., accounting vs shipping)
Every department must get identical irrelevant content only

explanation: Role-based training matches real job risks.

prompt: Third parties who need training can include…

options.text: Contractors, partners, suppliers, and others connecting to your network/services

explanation: Anyone from outside on your systems needs appropriate security training too.

prompt: Organizations should track training completion so that…

options.text: You know who has a baseline understanding and who still needs training

explanation: Completion tracking proves coverage across the user population.

prompt: Security policies should be…

options.text: Documented and easy to find (intranet) and included in the employee handbook

explanation: People can’t follow what they can’t find.

prompt: Situational awareness for users means…

options.text: Constantly watching for threats in day-to-day work (email, URLs, texts, physical media)
Only caring about security once a year
Clicking every link to verify it

explanation: Phishing, smishing, odd URLs, and “official” USB drops are all in scope.

prompt: An “official-looking” envelope containing a USB drive should make users…

options.text: Think twice — don’t plug unknown USB media into work computers
Share it with coworkers to test

explanation: Physical delivery of malware via USB is a real social-engineering path.

prompt: Insider threats are hard to identify, so training/ops should emphasize…

options.text: Only external firewalls with no internal checks
A multi-factor approach — multiple approvals, file monitoring, hard-to-bypass controls

explanation: Layered controls catch misuse that single checks miss.

prompt: Password requirements taught to users are often enforced by…

options.text: Sharing one password for the whole team
Administrative policy (e.g., Windows Group Policy for length/complexity)

explanation: Teach the standard — then enforce it technically.

prompt: User training on removable media/cables commonly warns that…

options.text: Removable media is out of scope for Security+
Any cable found in an airport is always safe
Unknown USBs can deliver malware, and random public charging cables can be risky

explanation: Physical connectors are attack paths — especially away from the office.

prompt: For social engineering, users should be trained to…

options.text: Only report after data is already stolen
Recognize it, understand what’s happening, and report it to IT security
Always give out credentials to helpful callers

explanation: Identify → understand → report; also protect sensitive data and think from an attacker’s view.

prompt: Remote/home workers add risk because…

options.text: Family/friends may use work systems; devices are outside the building; VPN access needs stronger controls

explanation: Train: no sharing work devices, extra endpoint protection, hardened remote access.
